summary: An informational memo describing how Sun's SKIP protocol lets a Mobile IP node roaming outside its home network negotiate access past a firewall.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2356 describes how a laptop that has travelled away from its office network can get back in through the office firewall, and how the traffic can be protected on the way. It uses SKIP, a protocol that protects each packet without a prior negotiation.

questions: how does mobile ip work through a firewall
what is the mobile ip traversal extension
why use skip instead of socks for mobile ip
subtitle: How a roaming Mobile IP laptop can negotiate its way past a SKIP firewall into its home network.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP provides no security for data traffic, and a mobile node roaming on the public Internet cannot simply reach its private home network through the firewall.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile node wraps its Mobile IP registration and data packets in SKIP headers addressed to the firewall, which authenticates it, relays the packets inward and sets up a dynamic binding for traffic coming back. An optional Traversal Extension names the firewalls on the path.
tldr.outcome: A roaming node gets a secure channel into its home network. The memo is Informational and leaves open how a node discovers the firewalls on its path.

today: RFC 2356 is an Informational memo from June 1998, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 2002 for Mobile IP, and the text notes that it does not solve the firewall discovery problem.

sections.title: The Problem, the Players and the Firewall's Limits
sections.content:
The Mobile IP specification establishes the mechanisms that let a mobile host keep the same IP address as it changes its point of attachment. Mobility implies higher security risks than static operation, because the traffic may at times take unforeseen network paths with unknown or unpredictable security characteristics, and the Mobile IP specification makes no provision for securing data traffic. The mechanisms in this document let a mobile node out on a public part of the Internet negotiate access past a SKIP firewall and construct a secure channel into its home network. They also let it roam into regions that impose ingress filtering and use a different address space.

The document describes what support is needed at the firewall, the Mobile IP home agent and the mobile node, for example so that an employee can attach a laptop to a PPP or SLIP account at an Internet service provider, or to a 10Base-T network in a terminal room or another company's premises. The relevant interface is configured with an IP address different from the one used at the office, and that address may be assigned temporarily and dynamically, by IPCP in the PPP case or by DHCP in the 10Base-T case.

The setting is a private network separated by a firewall from the general Internet. The private network may use a private address space whose addresses are not even routable by the general Internet. The mobile node has its permanent address inside the private network but connects from elsewhere, and as Mobile IP defines, it uses a care-of address while roaming. The home agent serves as a location registry and router, the foreign agent as a registration relayer and source of the care-of address, and the correspondent node is the system exchanging data with the mobile node. The firewall enforces access control between the private network and the Internet, perhaps by a combination of application gatewaying, packet filtering and cryptographic techniques.

The firewall imposes restrictions on packets entering or leaving the private network: a packet is not allowed through unless it conforms to a filtering specification, or unless there is a negotiation involving some sort of authentication. A second restriction comes from the separation between private and public addresses. Strictly speaking this is not imposed by the firewall but by the character of the private network: a packet destined for an internal address that originates in the general Internet will probably not be delivered, not because the firewall drops it but because the Internet's routing fabric cannot process it, which elicits an ICMP host unreachable packet back to the sender. Because of this, the firewall must be explicitly targeted as the destination node by outside packets seeking to enter the private network; the routing fabric will only see the public address of the firewall, and once the packet arrives there the real packet is recovered.
sections.plainLanguage: A laptop that travels takes its address with it, but the office firewall and the office address range stay behind. The laptop has to knock on the firewall's door, be recognised, and have its packets carried inside.

sections.title: Two Firewall Options: SOCKS and SKIP
sections.content:
The memo examines two ways a firewall could support mobile nodes: application relaying or proxying, and IP Security. It looks at two specific schemes, SOCKS version 5 and SKIP.

The SOCKS solution, from the IETF's authenticated firewall traversal working group, requires the mobile node, or another node on its behalf, to establish a TCP session with the firewall to exchange UDP traffic with it, and to use the SOCKS library to encapsulate the traffic. The steps are a TCP connection to port 1080, which takes 1.5 round trips, then a version identifier and method selection negotiation taking 1 round trip, then a method-dependent negotiation, where username and password authentication takes 1 round trip and GSS-API negotiation requires at least 3 round trips, and finally the SOCKS request and reply taking 1 round trip. That is a minimum of 4 round trips, or 6 with GSS-API, before the client can pass data through the firewall. The memo notes that all of this must be done each time the mobile node registers a new care-of address, that the scheme requires UDP to encapsulate IP datagrams, and that SOCKS defines how to establish authenticated connections but does not provide a clear solution to encrypting the traffic.

The SKIP alternative encrypts and authenticates the traffic from the mobile node to the firewall with a session-less IP security mechanism, which removes the need to set up a session just to exchange UDP traffic. The memo finds this very attractive, because no round trip times are incurred before the mobile node and the firewall achieve mutual trust: the firewall can start relaying packets for the mobile node as soon as it receives the first one. That implies SKIP is used with the IP Authentication Header so that authentication information is in each packet, and encryption with ESP is also assumed because the Internet at large is considered a hostile environment; an ESP transform providing both authentication and encryption could be used instead, in which case the AH header is not needed.

The firewall and the mobile node may be previously configured with each other's authenticated Diffie-Hellman public components, or they may exchange them in real time using one of the mechanisms the SKIP protocol defines. Home agents and the firewall must likewise have or be able to exchange each other's public components. The memo notes that other proposals for IP layer security are session-oriented and typically imply negotiations spanning several round trips before cryptographically secure communications are possible, which raises the same concerns as the SOCKS approach.

SKIP also supports nomadic applications. Two hosts using a secure IP layer channel normally use the IP source and destination addresses on incoming packets to arrive at the right security association, and the SKIP header can supersede that by including the key ID the recipient must use to obtain the right certificate. That key ID is given by two fields, a name space identifier and a master key identifier that uniquely indicates, within that name space, the id to use in fetching the proper certificate. Setting the name space identifier to 1 and the master key ID to the home address tells a receiver to ignore the IP source and use the home address to look up the public component, and setting it to 8 enables Unsigned Diffie-Hellman certificates, where the master key ID is the MD5 hash of the Diffie-Hellman public component. Mobile IP is best supported by a nomadic access control list entry at the SKIP firewall, an entry filtered by key ID instead of by IP source address, which translates to allowing access from any IP source address for a given name space and master key ID combination. Incoming packets must have an AH header, so that after authenticating them the firewall establishes a current address, or dynamic binding, for the nomadic host. This supports Mobile IP because the mobile node always initiates contact, giving the firewall a chance to learn its current address before encrypting an outgoing packet. It does preclude simultaneous bindings, because the last Registration Request replaces the association between the permanent address and any prior care-of address; supporting those would require the firewall to interpret Mobile IP registration messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The alternative to a firewall that relays applications is a firewall that simply protects packets. The first needs a long conversation before any data flows; the second needs none, because every packet carries its own proof of who sent it.

sections.title: Secure Channel Configurations
sections.content:
The mobile node takes part in two kinds of traffic, the Mobile IP registration protocol and data, and the memo evaluates secure channel configurations by looking at the initial Registration Request sent to the home agent. Assuming the mobile node operates with a co-located address, it can communicate directly with the firewall, the firewall can reach the home agent inside the private network, and the firewall must be able to authenticate the mobile node.

Configuration I encrypts only between the mobile node out on the general Internet and the firewall's external interface. This is the minimum required, and the memo calls it the most desirable configuration, because the more expensive encrypted channel is used only where it is necessary, on the public network. Configuration II extends the encrypted tunnel through the firewall, so the firewall is limited to a simple relay or gateway function. The memo says this is probably unrealizable in practice, because it is unlikely to be popular with computer security personnel, since authentication would be carried out by the home agent rather than by the firewall, and the home agent's security is potentially much weaker. Configuration III allows the firewall to be party to the security association between the home agent and the mobile node: after verifying the AH header, the firewall forwards the encrypted packet to the home agent. The memo says this implies the participating entities disclose their pairwise long-term Diffie-Hellman shared secret to the intermediate node, and calls it unsavory to the end user, while configuration II is probably not agreeable to security and system administration personnel. Configuration IV encrypts traffic on the public network and on the private network, with a security association between the mobile node and the firewall outside and one between the home agent and the firewall inside.

A potential problem in configurations II and III is that their end-to-end channel components assume the mobile node and the home agent can exchange IP traffic directly, which is generally not the case, because the Internet routing fabric may not have routes to private addresses and the private routing fabric may ignore or be restricted from routing to public addresses. Packets therefore have to be addressed directly to the firewall and indirectly to the real destination on the other side. Configurations I and IV are essentially equivalent, and the memo notes that the latter may be considered overkill because it encrypts even within the private network, which is generally unnecessary; what is needed inside the private network is for the home agent to add an encapsulation, not necessarily encrypted, to direct datagrams to the mobile node via the firewall, which the memo says is obtainable with IP in IP encapsulation. The difference is that configuration I does not protect data from eavesdroppers inside the private network, which may be unacceptable when traffic from some departments, such as payroll or legal, crosses other parts of the company. In the interest of being conservative the memo assumes configuration IV. It also notes that because the firewall is party to the security associations on both networks it can always inspect the traffic, and that if this is a concern the home agent and mobile node could set up a bi-directional tunnel and encrypt it.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four places to put the encryption: only on the public network, straight from the laptop to the home agent, with the firewall in the middle checking, or on both networks. The memo settles on protecting both networks, and explains what each other choice costs.

sections.title: Registration and Data Transfer
sections.content:
When roaming within a private network, the mobile node sends Registration Requests directly to its home agent. On the public Internet it must encapsulate the original Registration Request in a SKIP packet destined to the firewall. The mobile node must distinguish between inside and outside addresses, which could be done by rules defining the address ranges, though actual installations may present serious difficulties in defining exactly what is a private address and what is not. Direct human input is effective, since it may be obvious to the user that the current point of attachment is outside the private network. The home agent must also distinguish between the two, and lacks the benefit of direct user input, so the memo defines a Traversal Extension to carry that knowledge in Registration Requests and Replies. Because errors in judgement are to be expected, the firewall should be configured to keep relaying even when a mobile node with an inside care-of address asks it to.

The rule for whether to use SKIP is not a simple one keyed on a destination address. It applies when the mobile node is using a care-of address that does not belong to the private network and either the source address of the packet is the mobile node's home address, or the source address is the care-of address and the destination address belongs to the private network. Because these conditions are mobility related, it is best for the Mobile IP function in the node to evaluate them and then request the appropriate security services from SKIP.

On the outside network, the SKIP module uses the firewall's destination address and certificate to address and encrypt the packet, with SKIP combined with ESP and possibly AH. The SKIP header's source name space identifier equals 1, indicating that the master key ID is the mobile node's home address, while the IP packet's source address is the care-of address, whose public component is unknown to the firewall. Inside the private network, the firewall's dynamic packet filtering establishes a dynamic binding between the care-of address and the mobile node's permanent home address. The destination name space identifier is zero, which prompts the firewall to process the SKIP header and recover the internal packet, which it then delivers to another outbound interface because it is addressed to the home agent, encrypting it with SKIP before forwarding under configuration IV.

The home agent examines the care-of address reported by the mobile node and, if it is an outside address, sends all traffic back through the firewall by encapsulating the Registration Reply in a SKIP packet destined to the firewall. On the outside, the firewall recovers the original reply and, using the dynamic binding set up by the original Registration Request, encrypts it with the mobile node's public component. This dynamic binding capability and the use of tunnelling mode ESP remove the need to extend Mobile IP with a relay Registration Request, but require the Registration Reply to leave the private network through the same firewall that forwarded the Request. A Mobile IP aware firewall could instead take the permanent address from the Registration Reply itself, which renders the firewall stateless and lets Requests and Replies traverse the periphery of the private network through different firewalls.

Data transfer proceeds along similar lines. A data packet from the mobile node to a correspondent node inside the private network has the same shape as the Registration Request, with the source address the care-of address, the destination the firewall's public address, and the inner IP header running from the mobile node's home address to the correspondent node. The firewall decrypts the inner header and payload, checks the destination address, and delivers the inner datagram internally, after which it is routed independently of its source address. Since that assumption is not always true, the mobile node may construct a bi-directional tunnel with its home agent, which guarantees that the inner IP header runs from the care-of address to the home agent. On the way back, the home agent intercepts the packet from the correspondent node, encapsulates it so that the Mobile IP header runs from the home agent to the care-of address, and sends it via the firewall in a SKIP packet. The dynamic packet filter configured by the original Registration Request triggers the encryption of that packet by the firewall for the mobile node, and the mobile node finally recovers the inner IP header and the upper-layer payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The first thing the laptop does when it lands somewhere new is register with its home agent, and it does that by sending the registration to the firewall wrapped in protection. The firewall checks it, learns where the laptop now is, and passes it inside. Everything afterwards follows the same path, in both directions.

sections.title: The Traversal Extension
sections.content:
The Traversal Extension may be included by mobile nodes in Registration Requests and by home agents in Registration Replies, and must appear before the Mobile-Home Authentication Extension. It is an explicit notification that there are one or more traversal points, such as firewalls or fireridges, between the mobile node and its home agent. Negotiating access past these systems may imply a new authentication header and possibly a new encapsulating header, perhaps as part of tunnelling mode ESP, whose IP destination address is the traversal address. Negotiating access past traversal points does not necessarily require cryptographic techniques: systems at the boundary between separate address spaces must be explicitly targeted, perhaps using unencrypted IP in IP encapsulation.

A mobile node should include one Traversal Extension per traversal point in its Registration Requests, and if several are present their order must exactly match the order in which packets encounter them as they flow from the mobile node towards the home agent. There may be additional firewalls along the way, but the list should only include those systems with which an explicit negotiation is required. The home agent should likewise include one extension per traversal point in its Replies, in the order the packets encounter them on the way back.

A Traversal Extension does not include any indication of how access is negotiated, and that information is presumably obtained through separate means. The memo says explicitly that it does not attempt to solve the firewall discovery problem, that is, it does not specify how to discover the list of traversal points. Because the type value falls within the range 128 to 255, a home agent or mobile node that meets a Traversal Extension may silently ignore it, which is consistent with the extension being essentially a hint.

The extension itself is a fixed layout: a type of 129, a length of 10, a reserved field of 0, an MN to HA Traversal Address and an HA to MN Traversal Address. The MN to HA field holds the IP address of an intermediate system or firewall encountered by datagrams sent by the mobile node towards the home agent, typically the external address of a firewall, and must be initialised in Registration Requests. In Registration Replies it is typically all zeros, otherwise the mobile node should interpret it as a hint. The HA to MN field holds the address of a system encountered by datagrams sent by the home agent towards the mobile node, typically the internal address of a firewall, and must be initialised in Registration Replies, while in Registration Requests it is typically all zeros.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension is a note attached to the registration that names the firewalls on the way, so the home agent knows where to send the reply. It says nothing about how the laptop found them, and the memo does not solve that problem.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says the topic of the document is security, but that it is imperative to point out the perils involved in allowing a flow of IP packets through a firewall. In essence, the mobile host itself must also take on responsibility for securing the private network, because it extends its periphery. This does not mean it stops exchanging unencrypted IP packets with hosts on the public network; it may have to do so to satisfy billing requirements imposed by the foreign site, or to renew its DHCP lease. In the latter case the firewall might filter not only on IP source address but also on protocol and port numbers. Therefore, the mobile host must have some firewall capabilities, otherwise any malicious individual who gains access to it will have gained access to the private network as well.
sections.plainLanguage: A laptop that is let inside the firewall is now a door into the office network, so it has to keep its own defences. The memo is blunt about that.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Extension type. A value in 128 to 255 means it may be ignored.

fields.name: MN to HA Traversal Address
fields.desc: Firewall met by packets going from the mobile node toward the home agent.

fields.name: HA to MN Traversal Address
fields.desc: Firewall met by packets going from the home agent toward the mobile node.

items.title: I: encryption outside only
items.text: Encrypted on the public network only. The minimum required.

items.title: II: end-to-end encryption
items.text: The tunnel runs through the firewall. The firewall only relays.

items.title: III: end-to-end with intermediate authentication
items.text: The firewall checks the packet and forwards it encrypted.

items.title: IV: encryption inside and outside
items.text: Encrypted on the public network and inside the private network.
